summary: The BGP MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED) attribute lets a network tell a neighbor which entry point into its network is best. It works in many cases but can cause problems in dynamic or complex topologies. This document discusses implementation and deployment considerations for implementers and operators. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A city tells visitors which gate to use. Usually that helps, but sometimes it causes confusing traffic jams. This note explains what to watch for.

questions: hot potato vs cold potato routing
subtitle: Pitfalls and best practices for using BGP's MED attribute in routing.

tldr.problem: The BGP MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED) attribute tells neighboring networks which entry point into your network is best, but it has complex behavior and can cause routing problems in dynamic or complex topologies.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents how the MED attribute works per the BGP specification, then catalogs implementation inconsistencies and practical deployment issues that arise when using MEDs. It provides guidance for implementers and operators on when MEDs cause problems.
tldr.outcome: Network operators now have a detailed reference for the pitfalls of MED use: comparing MEDs across different autonomous systems, route flap damping interactions, effects on route reflection and confederations, and unexpected routing behavior. Knowing these issues helps avoid misconfiguration.

today: RFC 4451 is Informational and remains current guidance for BGP operations. It documents deployment and implementation considerations for MED use. While the MED attribute is still part of the BGP specification and is used in production networks, most operators follow the conservative practices this RFC recommends: resetting MEDs on ingress, not propagating them into IBGP, or avoiding them entirely.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The BGP MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED) attribute is an optional, non-transitive attribute used on external (EBGP) links to signal the best entry point into an autonomous system to neighbors. While MEDs work correctly in many scenarios, their use can lead to routing issues in dynamic or complex topologies. This RFC documents both implementation and deployment considerations that network operators and equipment makers should understand. The document distinguishes between implementation advice (what BGP speakers should do) and deployment advice (how operators should use MEDs in production networks), acknowledging that the two sometimes conflict.
sections.eli5: BGP's MED attribute tells neighbors which way into your network is best. But it can cause weird routing problems if you're not careful. This guide explains what goes wrong and how to avoid it.

sections.title: How MED Works
sections.content: The MED attribute is a 32-bit unsigned number that indicates preference for an exit point. Per the BGP specification, lower MED values are preferred, and MEDs are only compared between routes learned from the same neighboring autonomous system. When you receive a MED over EBGP, you may optionally propagate it to IBGP peers and modify it; you must not send it to other EBGP neighbors. Two routing strategies emerge: hot potato routing (closest-exit) minimizes transit traffic by not propagating EBGP MEDs into IBGP, while cold potato routing (best-exit) uses the neighbor's MED to route to the point the neighbor advertised as best. In practice, many deployments behave like "mashed potatoes"—not hot or cold, but confused—because of MED misconfigurations.
sections.eli5: The MED number tells your neighbors which door is best. Lower numbers are better. Hot potato means "drop it and use the closest door." Cold potato means "trust the neighbor's choice." Mashed potatoes means nobody knows what's happening.

sections.title: Implementation Quirks and Issues
sections.content: Several implementation inconsistencies plague MED use. Different BGP implementations send MEDs to IBGP neighbors by default or not, leading to suboptimal route selection within an AS. Some implementations treat a missing MED as 0 (the minimum), while others treat it as infinity (2^32-1); the current BGP spec says missing MEDs should be treated as 0, but older versions differed. Some implementations use 2^32-1 internally as "infinity" and rewrite that value to 2^32-2 on receipt, creating unexpected routing changes. Some implementations allow MED comparisons between routes from different autonomous systems, which can cause side effects. The MED is non-transitive, so behavior at route reflectors and confederations can introduce persistent route oscillations. As a workaround, many operators reset all MEDs to a fixed value on ingress to avoid relying on consistent missing-MED behavior across routers.
sections.eli5: Different routers have different ideas about what MED means. Some ignore the neighbor's number. Some treat a missing number as the best or worst. Some routers argue about which door is best and keep changing their minds. Most operators just ignore MED and pick their own door.

sections.title: Deployment Pitfalls
sections.content: In production networks, accepting MEDs from other autonomous systems allows those operators to influence your routing decisions, effectively allowing them to traffic engineer your network. If a BGP session resets, MEDs can change dramatically, leading to sudden traffic reroutes and congestion. Dynamically derived MEDs (computed from IGP metrics) can cause BGP route flap damping to suppress routes whenever internal topology changes occur, even if the external route is still good. When aggregating routes, using MED values from different aggregation points creates suboptimal routing. Comparing MEDs between different autonomous systems often produces unexpected results because different networks use different IGP protocols with different metric spaces (OSPF vs. IS-IS). Route reflectors and confederations can introduce persistent route oscillation when MEDs are used, because the non-hierarchical nature of MED comparisons conflicts with the hierarchical aggregation these scaling mechanisms provide.
sections.eli5: Using the neighbor's hint means they can mess with your traffic. If they change their mind, your network gets congested. If your routers keep changing their internal costs, you'll confuse the other networks. When you combine routes from different places, the hints get worse. Adding too many layers of routers can make them flip-flop forever.

sections.title: Best Practices
sections.content: The RFC recommends that operators should be aware of these issues before using MEDs. Many operators explicitly reset MEDs on ingress and avoid using MED values of 0 and 2^32-1 to sidestep implementation inconsistencies. Not propagating EBGP MEDs into IBGP (hot potato routing) significantly reduces oscillation risk. If you must compare MEDs between different autonomous systems, use LOCAL_PREF instead to make preference explicit. Do not modify MED attributes on IBGP sessions; even though it may be technically allowed, it risks creating route loops. Document your MED policy clearly, including whether you use hot or cold potato routing for each peer or traffic class. Test MED behavior thoroughly in your network before deploying it widely.
sections.eli5: If you use MED, be very careful. Treat all hints the same value to simplify things. Drop the hints when passing them inside your network. Use your own preference settings instead. Don't experiment with MED once it's live; test it first. Write down exactly how you use it so other engineers understand.

viz.caption: Hot potato vs. cold potato routing

left.title: Hot Potato (Closest-Exit)
left.desc: Do not propagate EBGP MED into IBGP. Use the closest peering point regardless of neighbor's hint.

right.title: Cold Potato (Best-Exit)
right.desc: Propagate EBGP MED into IBGP. Use the neighbor's advertised best entry point.
